issues.legal_issue: The character of a religious endowment as public or private is determined by the founder’s intended beneficiaries and the surrounding evidence of the endowment’s use, management, and support.
material_facts: The founder intended the deity to be worshipped continually by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public and arranged for regular worship, devotional singing, ceremonies, and processions.
The public worshipped at the temple over a long period without evidence of hindrance or restriction.
The temple received a government land grant in its own name and was managed by successive spiritual successors as managers rather than as personal owners.
Members of the public donated land and contributed subscriptions for worship and ceremonies.
The institution was held out and treated by its managers as a place for public use, and its history contained no evidence that it had been treated as private property.
issues.conclusion: The endowment was a public trust, not a private religious endowment.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(13) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, a public trust includes an express or constructive trust for a public religious purpose; section 2(17) defines a temple by its use as a place of public religious worship and dedication to, benefit of, or use as of right by the Hindu community or a section of it. The distinction between public and private trusts turns principally on whether the beneficiaries are the general public or an unascertained class, rather than specified or ascertainable individuals, and whether the founder intended the public or a specified portion of it to have the right of worship. Public use without interference is cogent evidence of dedication. The court may also consider the temple’s origin, management, grants and gifts, devotees’ worship rights, and the awareness of managers and devotees of its public character; not every factor must be present. The court relied on Deoki Nandan v. Murlidhar, State of Bihar v. Charusila Dasi, Narayan Bhagwantrao Gosavi Balajiwale v. Gopal Vinayak Gosavi, Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan, Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhodas Kalidas, and Bihar State Board Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das.

predicates.religious_endowment_classification_proce: The dispute concerns whether a religious endowment is public or private.
predicates.founder_intended_worship_for_indetermina: The founder intended the place or deity to be worshipped by an indeterminate body of public worshippers.
predicates.public_worship_without_interference: Members of the public worshipped at the place over time without interference or restriction.
predicates.public_contributions_supported_worship: Members of the public gave gifts or contributions to support worship or related ceremonies.
predicates.government_grant_recognized_temple_endow: A government grant identified the temple or religious institution as the holder or beneficiary of endowed property.
predicates.succession_managers_treated_property_as_: Successive managers administered the property for the religious institution rather than as their personal property.

issues.definition: When a religious-endowment classification proceeding establishes public worship intended by the founder, or public worship without interference supported by evidence of public dedication or trust management, the endowment is classified as public.

issues.legal_issue: Restricting who may perform inner rituals does not by itself make a temple private when the public is admitted to worship through darshan.
material_facts: The public could visit the temple for darshan and offerings, while the daily performance of puja in the inner sanctum was carried out by the appointed worshipper and others could not perform puja without permission.
The temple was intended for public darshan and had a long history of worship by the public.
issues.conclusion: The restriction on public performance of puja did not establish that the temple was private.
issues.legal_principle: In deciding whether a temple is public, the court considers public access for darshan, participation in worship and festivals, and other evidence of the temple’s character. Public worshippers need not themselves be permitted to perform the daily rituals in the inner sanctum; limitation of those rituals to appointed worshippers does not negate public character. The court relied on Tilkayat Shri Govindlalji Maharaj v. State of Rajasthan and Goswami Shri Mahalaxmi Vahuji v. Rannchhodas Kalidas.

predicates.public_or_private_temple_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a place of worship is a public or private temple.
predicates.public_admitted_for_darshan: Members of the public are admitted to visit the place of worship for darshan.
predicates.inner_rituals_limited_to_authorized_wors: Performance of rituals in the inner sanctum is restricted to appointed or otherwise authorized worshippers.

issues.definition: When a public-or-private temple dispute involves public admission for darshan but inner rituals limited to authorized worshippers, that ritual restriction does not make the temple private.
